nameStory: This rare mountain wildflower is named after William Dandridge Peck, an American naturalist who first discovered it growing on Mount Washington in 1804. The 'Eastern' part of its name distinguishes it from similar western mountain avens, while 'avens' comes from an old Latin word for a type of healing herb.
description: Eastern Mountain Avens is a small, low-growing perennial wildflower that forms compact clumps in rocky mountain areas. This member of the rose family produces cheerful yellow flowers on short stems above a rosette of deeply divided leaves. The entire plant typically grows only 6-12 inches tall, perfectly adapted to harsh mountain conditions where it hugs the ground to avoid strong winds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with 5 rounded petals that feel slightly papery when touched, blooming from June to August on short, sturdy stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed, compound leaves arranged in a basal rosette that feels somewhat fuzzy and rough to the touch, with smaller leaflets mixed between larger ones

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, dense mats or cushions that rarely exceed one foot in height, spreading slowly outward from a central crown

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops clusters of small, dry fruits with long, feathery tails that catch the wind and feel soft and silky when brushed

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Found only in extremely rocky, exposed alpine areas above treeline where few other flowering plants can survive the harsh conditions

habitat: Eastern Mountain Avens exists in only the most extreme alpine environments in New England, specifically on exposed rocky slopes and cliff faces above treeline in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. It thrives in thin, gravelly soils between granite boulders where snow lingers late into spring. You'll find it in areas so harsh that only specialized alpine plants like diapensia and mountain sandwort can survive alongside it.

seasonality.spring: Leaves begin emerging from snow-covered rocky crevices in late May or early June, appearing as small green rosettes pressed close to the rocks.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom from mid-June through August, creating dramatic splashes of color against the gray granite landscape.
seasonality.fall: Feathery seed heads develop and disperse in the mountain winds, while leaves may take on reddish tints before going dormant.
seasonality.winter: Plants retreat into protected rock crevices, completely dormant and invisible under deep snow and ice for 6-7 months.

funFact: Eastern Mountain Avens is one of North America's rarest wildflowers, existing in only five locations worldwide - three spots in Nova Scotia and just two places in New Hampshire's White Mountains, making it more geographically restricted than many endangered animals!
confusionNotes: Could potentially be confused with other yellow mountain wildflowers like mountain avens buttercup, but the deeply divided, compound leaves in a basal rosette and the extremely limited alpine habitat above treeline make identification fairly straightforward - if you're seeing it, you're probably in one of the only places it grows!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Eastern' Mountain Avens, this plant is actually more closely related to western mountain species than to other eastern avens, suggesting it's a relict population left behind from colder ice age climates when such plants were more widespread.
compareHints: Unlike its avens relatives that grow in woodlands and meadows, Eastern Mountain Avens is the only species in its genus adapted to extreme alpine conditions in New England. While Water Avens has drooping, bell-shaped flowers and grows near streams, and White Avens has tiny white flowers in forests, Eastern Mountain Avens stands apart with its bright yellow blooms and rock-hugging alpine lifestyle.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's avens species, white avens is distinguished by its small white petals and grabby seed heads.
Water Avens stands out among its relatives by being the wetland specialist with drooping flowers.
Among New England's avens species, yellow avens is the most common and widespread.
Rough avens is the scruffiest member of the New England avens family, with the most noticeably hairy and rough-textured leaves.
Among New England's avens, Large-leaved Avens is the champion of seed dispersal with its aggressively clingy fruit balls.
Wood Avens differs from our native White Avens by having yellow flowers instead of white ones and preferring shadier spots.
Among New England's avens species, Spring Avens stands out for its early bloom time and preference for consistently moist, rich soils.

Among New England's avens species, cream-colored avens stands out for its distinctly pale yellow to cream flowers - white avens has pure white petals, yellow avens has bright yellow ones, and water avens has drooping, bell-shaped flowers.

Unlike other New England avens which typically have upward-facing yellow or white flowers, prairie smoke has distinctive nodding pinkish flowers and creates the dramatic feathery seed plumes that no other regional avens species produce.

Scarlet Avens stands out dramatically from all other New England avens species primarily due to its bright red flowers - our native avens species like White Avens, Water Avens, and Yellow Avens all have much more subdued flower colors.
